slides.title: Loans and Credit Basics
slides.kicker: Borrowing can build you up or pull you down
bullets: Sometimes people need to borrow money from banks, relatives, or other sources as loans.
Borrowing or using credit is helpful when it is used for productive purposes, but it becomes harmful if misused.
An education loan can help a student pursue higher education and build a better future.
Borrowing for unnecessary consumer goods may lead to a debt burden and financial difficulties.
slides.note: Credit ek tool hai — use it to build, not to splurge!

slides.title: Borrow Responsibly
slides.kicker: Two simple rules before you sign any loan
bullets: Responsible borrowing means taking loans only when they are truly necessary.
Before borrowing, make sure the loan can be repaid on time.
Debt is the amount of money owed to somebody, and unplanned debt grows stressful fast.

slides.title: What Is an EMI
bullets: An EMI (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed amount of money a person pays every month to repay a loan.
Each EMI includes a portion of the original loan amount, called the principal.
It also includes the interest charged by the lender for letting you use the money.
slides.note: EMI = principal + interest, every single month.

slides.title: Fridge on EMI Example
bullets: A family wants a refrigerator costing ₹30,000 but does not want to pay the entire amount at once.
They take a loan and repay it through an EMI of ₹3,000 every month for 12 months.
EMIs are commonly used to purchase mobile phones, household appliances, two-wheelers, homes, and cars.
slides.note: 12 x 3000 = 36000. The extra ₹6,000 is the cost of credit.

slides.title: EMI Trade-offs to Weigh
slides.kicker: Too many EMIs can eat your savings
bullets: Buying on EMI spreads a big cost over months, even though it may cost more in the long run.
Having too many EMIs can squeeze monthly savings and emergency funds.
So count your EMIs before adding one more, and borrow only what you can repay on time.
slides.note: Ek EMI plan karo, paanch nahi!

slides.title: Four Factors Before Investing
slides.kicker: Check these before money goes anywhere
bullets: When deciding where to invest money, consider four factors: risk, return, time horizon, and liquidity.
Risk is the chance of losing money, and return is the profit earned from an investment.
Time horizon is how long money can remain invested, and liquidity is how easily an asset becomes cash.
slides.note: Four boxes to tick before you invest.

slides.title: Options: Risk Ladder
slides.kicker: FDs climb low, shares climb high
bullets: Fixed deposits are generally low-risk options that provide steady but relatively lower returns.
Mutual funds may offer higher returns than fixed deposits.
Shares (equity) have the potential to generate the highest returns over the long term, but they involve the highest level of risk.

right.title: Higher risk, higher potential
items: Mutual funds: may offer higher returns
Shares: highest potential returns, highest risk

slides.note: Ladder socho: FD, then mutual funds, then shares.

slides.title: The Risk-Return Trade-off
bullets: In general, lower-risk investments tend to offer lower returns.
Higher-risk investments may offer higher returns, but nothing is guaranteed.
The book draws this as a trade-off: low risk goes with low return, higher risk with higher potential return.
slides.note: Bigger returns ka promise, bigger risk ke saath aata hai.

slides.title: Choose What Fits You
bullets: People should choose investments based on their financial goals.
Also consider the amount of risk you are willing to take.
And think about when you are likely to need the money.

items: Check when you need the money

slides.title: What Taxes Are
slides.kicker: Everyone chips in for the country
bullets: Taxes are compulsory payments made by individuals and businesses to the government.
They fund public services such as schools, hospitals, transport, and defence.
Taxes also support other essential facilities that everyone in the country shares.

slides.title: Direct Taxes
bullets: Direct taxes are paid directly on a person's or organisation's income or profits.
Income tax is the book's example of a direct tax.
The person or organisation earning the income pays it straight to the government.
slides.note: Earner pays it directly — that is the 'direct'.

slides.title: Indirect Taxes
slides.kicker: Sitting quietly inside the price tag
bullets: Indirect taxes are added to the price of goods and services you buy.
The Goods and Services Tax (GST) is the book's example of an indirect tax.
You pay it every time you purchase taxed goods or services.

items: You buy a good or service
GST is added to its price

slides.note: Bill pe GST dekha? That is indirect tax.

slides.title: Direct vs Indirect
bullets: Both tax types fund public services, but they travel different routes to reach the government.
Direct tax: paid on income or profits, like income tax.
Indirect tax: added to the price of goods and services, like GST.

left.title: Direct taxes
items: Paid directly on income or profits

right.title: Indirect taxes
items: Added to price of goods and services
Paid at the time of purchase

slides.note: Salary pe income tax, shopping pe GST.

slides.title: Big Questions: Money Sense
slides.kicker: The book makes you argue it out
bullets: Why is managing money wisely important for all individuals, irrespective of their income?
How can budgeting help people balance present needs with future financial goals? Give examples.
Why is saving alone often not enough to build wealth, and how do investments increase the value of money over time?
slides.note: Answer in full sentences — examples ke saath.

slides.title: Big Questions: Choose Wisely
slides.kicker: Risk, insurance, and a big windfall
bullets: Is taking higher risks always the best way to earn higher returns? How should a person decide what suits them?
Why do people buy insurance policies even though they may never face a major loss?
The book ends by asking you to imagine your family receives ₹1,00,000 — plan it with budgeting, saving, investing, and insurance.
slides.note: There are no trick questions — only thoughtful answers.

slides.title: School Reopening Budget
bullets: Your parents have given you ₹3,000 to prepare for the new school year.
List the items you need and find their prices by visiting local stores or asking a parent or teacher, then prepare a budget.
If the total is under ₹3,000 you may add one additional item; if it exceeds ₹3,000, decide which items to postpone or avoid.
The book's template lists school bag, books, uniform and shoes, notebooks, pens, pencils, and art supplies.
slides.note: Accurate calculation mangta hai book — no guessing!

slides.title: Investment Planning Activity
bullets: You received cash gifts worth ₹3,000 on your last birthday and decided to save ₹1,500.
With your teacher, calculate returns for combinations like ₹500 in a fixed deposit, ₹800 in the stock market, and ₹200 in gold.
Use reliable sources such as newspapers, magazines, or official websites for returns of different options.
Then prepare an investment plan explaining why each option is suitable or unsuitable.
slides.note: Try other combinations bhi — compare karo.

slides.title: Plan a ₹1,00,000 Windfall
slides.kicker: One family, one lakh, many choices
bullets: The book imagines a family receiving ₹1,00,000 and asks how you would manage it.
Use the chapter's toolkit: budget the needs, keep savings for emergencies, and invest by goal and risk.
Protect the family with insurance, and borrow only for productive purposes that can be repaid on time.
slides.note: Sahi plan = budget + savings + smart investing.

examples.title: Refrigerator on EMI
examples.problem: A family buys a refrigerator costing ₹30,000. They do not want to pay the entire amount at once, so they take a loan and repay it through an EMI of ₹3,000 every month for 12 months. Find the total amount paid and the extra cost of buying on EMI.
steps: Each EMI carries a portion of the principal plus the interest charged by the lender.
Extra cost = ₹36,000 - ₹30,000 = ₹6,000, which is the cost of credit.
examples.answer: The family pays ₹36,000 in total, which is ₹6,000 more than the ₹30,000 cash price.

examples.title: School Reopening Budget of ₹3,000
examples.problem: Your parents give you ₹3,000 for the new school year. Using the book's template items (school bag, books, uniform and shoes, notebooks, pens, pencils, art supplies) with sample prices collected from local stores, prepare a budget and check that it stays within ₹3,000.
steps: Assign prices: bag ₹650, books ₹900, uniform and shoes ₹800, notebooks ₹250, pens ₹100, pencils ₹80, art supplies ₹120.
Since the total is under ₹3,000, the book allows adding one additional item of your choice, or the ₹100 can be written as savings.
examples.answer: Total expenses ₹2,900, within the ₹3,000 budget, leaving ₹100 as savings or one small extra item.

examples.title: Investing Birthday Gift Money
examples.problem: You received cash gifts worth ₹3,000 on your birthday and saved ₹1,500. You invest ₹500 in a fixed deposit at 8% a year (the same rate as the savings scheme in this chapter), ₹800 in the stock market, and ₹200 in gold. Suppose after one year the stock portion grows 10% and the gold portion grows 6% (sample rates for practice; real returns vary, so check reliable sources). Find the total value after one year.
steps: Fixed deposit: 8% of ₹500 = ₹40, so it becomes ₹540.
Gain = ₹1,632 - ₹1,500 = ₹132, about 8.8% in a year, while idle cash would still be ₹1,500.
examples.answer: The ₹1,500 grows to ₹1,632 in one year, a gain of ₹132, showing how investing can increase the value of money over time.
